en.statement: Bash passes $'a\tb' as one argument with a tab between a and b.
en.explanation: ANSI-C quoting decodes \t before Bash supplies the argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

en.statement: Bash removes the backslash from "a\q" when forming its argument.
en.explanation: A backslash before q stays literal inside double quotes, so the argument contains a backslash between a and q.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

en.statement: Bash parses a\ b as one command argument containing a space.
en.explanation: The unquoted backslash quotes the following space, keeping it inside the word.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting

en.statement: With x=mid, Bash expands pre"$x"'post' into the single argument premidpost.
en.explanation: Adjacent quoted and unquoted parts belong to the same word.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Quoting and Expansion

en.statement: With IFS=' ' and x=' a ', Bash gives empty arguments around a when expanding unquoted $x.
en.explanation: Bash discards IFS whitespace at the edges; this expansion supplies the argument a.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

en.statement: With IFS=: and x=a::b, Bash gives an empty argument between a and b when expanding unquoted $x.
en.explanation: Adjacent non-whitespace IFS delimiters produce an empty field.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

en.statement: With IFS='' and x='a b', Bash splits unquoted $x into separate a and b arguments.
en.explanation: An empty IFS disables word splitting, leaving a b as one argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

en.statement: With x='', Bash passes "" $x to a command as two empty arguments.
en.explanation: The explicit "" survives; the unquoted empty expansion disappears, leaving one empty argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Word Splitting

en.statement: With IFS=':,' and positional parameters a and b, Bash expands "$*" to the single argument a:,b.
en.explanation: Quoted "$*" uses the first IFS character between values, producing a:b.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Special Parameters

en.statement: With x='a *.cfg', Bash splits unquoted $x into two words before applying pathname expansion to them.
en.explanation: Word splitting comes before pathname expansion, so the unquoted value first becomes the words a and *.cfg, and Bash then matches *.cfg against filenames.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Expansion

en.statement: With x=';', Bash treats the semicolon produced by $x as a command separator.
en.explanation: Bash recognizes command syntax before expansion; the expanded semicolon is ordinary argument text.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Shell Grammar and Expansion

en.statement: With n=3, Bash expands {1..$n} into the words 1 2 3.
en.explanation: Brace expansion runs before parameter expansion, so $n does not become a sequence endpoint.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Brace Expansion

en.statement: Bash expands {b,a} into b followed by a in the written order.
en.explanation: Brace expansion generates textual alternatives in their written order.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Brace Expansion

en.statement: With HOME=/srv/me, Bash expands "~/cfg" into /srv/me/cfg.
en.explanation: The quoted tilde stays literal, so this argument is ~/cfg.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Tilde Expansion

en.statement: With x='a *', Bash stores a * literally when it executes the scalar assignment value=$x.
en.explanation: Scalar assignment values skip word splitting and pathname expansion.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameters

en.statement: With nullglob enabled, Bash removes an unmatched unquoted *.cfg argument from a command.
en.explanation: An unmatched pattern disappears from the command's argument list when nullglob is enabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

en.statement: With failglob enabled, Bash runs a command with an unmatched *.cfg pattern as a literal argument.
en.explanation: failglob reports an expansion error and prevents that command from executing.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

en.statement: With dotglob enabled and .env present, Bash includes .env among the matches for *.
en.explanation: dotglob permits * to match the initial dot in .env.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pathname Expansion

en.statement: In Bash 5.3, GLOBSORT=-name makes Bash sort pathname matches in ascending name order.
en.explanation: The leading minus reverses the name sort, so -name selects descending order.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: GLOBSORT

en.statement: Bash performs quote removal before pathname expansion when preparing a command's arguments.
en.explanation: Quote removal is the final expansion stage, after pathname expansion.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Expansion

en.statement: With x='', Bash expands ${x-fallback} to the empty value stored in x.
en.explanation: A null value still counts as set. Adding a colon to -, =, ? or + makes that operator test null values too.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x='', Bash assigns ready to x when it evaluates ${x:=ready}.
en.explanation: The := form stores its fallback in an unset or empty variable.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x='', Bash expands ${x:?missing} to missing and continues the command.
en.explanation: In a noninteractive shell, :? reports the supplied error text and exits with a nonzero status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x=ready, Bash expands ${x:+enabled} to the existing value ready.
en.explanation: The :+ form selects its alternate word, so this expansion produces enabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x=abcdef, Bash expands ${x:-2} to ef, the last two characters of x.
en.explanation: Written as ${x:-2}, this is the :- default-value operator; x is set and non-null, so the result is abcdef. A negative substring offset must be separated from the colon by a space, as in ${x: -2}.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x=a/b/c, Bash expands ${x##*/} to the remaining text b/c.
en.explanation: The ## form removes the longest matching prefix, a/b/, leaving c; # chooses the shortest match.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x=banana, Bash expands ${x//a/X} to bXnXnX by replacing the matching a characters.
en.explanation: The doubled slash applies the replacement to each matching a in the value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With x=ab, Bash changes x itself to AB when it expands ${x^^}.
en.explanation: The ^^ expansion yields AB while the stored value of x remains ab.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: With ordinary scalars x=ready and ref=x, Bash expands ${!ref} to ready.
en.explanation: Indirect expansion uses ref's value as the name of the parameter to read.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion

en.statement: Bash evaluates the division in $((7 / 2)) using integer arithmetic.
en.explanation: The arithmetic expansion truncates the integer quotient toward zero.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

en.statement: Bash requires declare -i before it evaluates a variable's value as an arithmetic expression.
en.explanation: An arithmetic operand's value is evaluated as an expression even when its variable lacks the integer attribute.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

en.statement: With x='', Bash rejects $((x + 1)) because x holds an empty string.
en.explanation: A null variable referenced by name evaluates to zero, so this expansion yields 1.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

en.statement: Bash reads 010 in arithmetic expansion as a decimal integer.
en.explanation: A leading zero selects octal notation, so 010 represents decimal eight.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation

en.statement: With n=1, Bash's $((n+=2)) expansion updates n in the current shell.
en.explanation: Arithmetic assignments inside an expansion modify the referenced variable; n becomes 3.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Evaluation and Arithmetic Expansion

en.statement: With stdout and stderr separate, Bash includes stderr text in the value captured by $(command).
en.explanation: This substitution captures standard output; standard error keeps its separate destination.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

en.statement: Bash preserves trailing newline characters in the value captured by "$(command)".
en.explanation: The $(...) form removes trailing newlines from captured standard output, including inside double quotes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

en.statement: Given a readable file f containing abc, Bash expands $(<f) to abc.
en.explanation: The $(<f) shorthand reads the file's contents into the substitution result.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

en.statement: In Bash 5.3, ${ x=changed; printf ok; } leaves x=changed in the calling shell.
en.explanation: This substitution runs in the current execution environment, so the assignment persists.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

en.statement: In Bash 5.3, ${| REPLY=ready; printf shown; } expands to shown.
en.explanation: The ${| ...; } form expands to REPLY, here ready; shown goes to the caller's standard output.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Substitution

en.statement: With declare -a a=(red blue), Bash puts red at index zero.
en.explanation: Implicit indices in an indexed compound assignment start at zero, so red occupies a[0].

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: With declare -A a, Bash accepts a['']=ready as an entry whose key is an empty string.
en.explanation: Associative array keys are nonempty strings, so this assignment fails instead of creating an empty-key entry.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=([2]=x [9]=y), Bash makes ${#a[@]} report the highest index plus one.
en.explanation: The expansion counts assigned elements, so this sparse array reports 2.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=([3]=yes), Bash expands ${a[1+2]} to the value yes.
en.explanation: Bash evaluates the indexed subscript as an arithmetic expression, selecting index 3.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=([2]=x [9]=y), Bash expands ${a[-8]} to the value stored at index 2.
en.explanation: Negative indexed subscripts count back from one greater than the maximum index, including gaps.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=([4]=x y), Bash places the unindexed value y at index zero.
en.explanation: Within this compound assignment, the omitted subscript follows the last assigned index, placing y at index 5.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=('red blue' ''), Bash supplies two arguments through "${a[@]}".
en.explanation: Quoted "${a[@]}" supplies one argument per element, retaining the embedded space and the empty element.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For associative a=([red]=x), Bash expands ${!a[@]} to the stored value x.
en.explanation: The ${!a[@]} expansion supplies assigned keys, so this array yields red.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=([2]=red [5]=blue [9]=green), Bash expands "${a[@]:2:2}" to red and blue arguments.
en.explanation: The offset starts at numeric index 2; the length selects two assigned elements despite the gaps.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays and Parameter Expansion

en.statement: For indexed a=(x y), Bash shifts y to index zero after unset 'a[0]'.
en.explanation: Unsetting an indexed element leaves surviving indices in place, so y remains at index 1.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: For indexed a=([3]=x), Bash expands the unsubscripted "$a" to the value x.
en.explanation: An unsubscripted array reference selects element 0. Since that element is unset here, "$a" yields an empty string.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays

en.statement: Bash selects the then branch when an if condition returns status zero.
en.explanation: An if command uses the condition's exit status to select its branch; zero selects the then list.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

en.statement: With value='a b', Bash treats $value as one operand in [[ $value == 'a b' ]].
en.explanation: Inside [[ ]], parameter expansions skip word splitting, leaving the embedded space inside the operand.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

en.statement: Bash gives [ -n ] a failure status because the string operand is absent.
en.explanation: The [ builtin sees the nonempty string -n as its single expression argument, so the test succeeds.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: test and [ Builtins

en.statement: With LC_ALL=C, Bash evaluates [[ 20 < 3 ]] as a successful string comparison.
en.explanation: The < operator compares strings lexically; the leading character 2 sorts before 3 in the C locale.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

en.statement: Bash compares the text 2+2 and 4 literally in [[ 2+2 -eq 4 ]].
en.explanation: Inside [[ ]], -eq evaluates its operands as arithmetic expressions, so 2+2 compares equal to 4.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

en.statement: Given an empty regular file f, Bash evaluates [[ -s f ]] as a successful file test.
en.explanation: The -s primary tests for a file whose size exceeds zero, so an empty regular file fails it.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

en.statement: Bash treats the right operand in [[ abc == a* ]] as a shell pattern.
en.explanation: The unquoted pattern a* matches abc, so this conditional expression succeeds.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

en.statement: With re='a.*', Bash matches abc in the expression [[ abc =~ "$re" ]].
en.explanation: Quoting "$re" makes the regex operand literal, so abc fails to match the literal text a.*.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

en.statement: After [[ abc123 =~ ([a-z]+)([0-9]+) ]], Bash sets BASH_REMATCH[0] to abc.
en.explanation: BASH_REMATCH[0] holds the whole matched substring, abc123. The first parenthesized group belongs to index 1.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

en.statement: With x=0, Bash leaves x at zero after [[ yes == yes || ++x -eq 1 ]].
en.explanation: The left comparison succeeds, so || skips the right expression and its increment.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

en.statement: Bash re-expands a for loop's in words between successive iterations.
en.explanation: Bash expands the item list before iteration begins; body changes leave that prepared list intact.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Loops

en.statement: Bash uses positional parameters as the items in for item; do :; done.
en.explanation: Omitting the in clause selects the positional parameters as the loop's iteration items.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Loops

en.statement: With item=old, Bash leaves item=new after for item in; do item=new; done.
en.explanation: An empty item list skips the body and makes no assignment to the loop variable, leaving item equal to old.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Loops

en.statement: Bash gives while false; do :; done an exit status of zero.
en.explanation: A while or until loop returns the status of the last body command it ran, or zero when the body never ran, so the failed condition's status is discarded.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands (while and until)

en.statement: Bash runs the body of until true; do :; done before evaluating its initial condition.
en.explanation: An until loop checks its condition first, so the initial successful true skips this body.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Loops

en.statement: Inside two nested Bash loops, break 2 resumes execution after the outer loop.
en.explanation: The numeric argument selects how many enclosing loops break terminates.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: break

en.statement: Inside two nested arithmetic for loops, Bash makes continue 2 run the outer loop's step expression.
en.explanation: The second enclosing loop resumes at its step expression, followed by its next condition check.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: continue and Arithmetic Loops

en.statement: With ;; clause terminators, Bash executes the last matching clause in a case command.
en.explanation: Bash examines clauses in source order; the first matching clause ending in ;; completes dispatch.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: case

en.statement: After a matching case clause, Bash's ;;& runs the next body before testing the next clause's pattern.
en.explanation: The ;;& terminator resumes pattern testing. The ;& terminator instead proceeds directly to the next body.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: case

en.statement: Bash treats the pattern "a"* in a case clause as the literal text a*.
en.explanation: Quoting part of a case pattern makes that part literal; the unquoted * stays active, so "a"* matches abc.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: case and Pattern Matching

en.statement: After f changes its arguments with set -- and returns, Bash restores the caller's positional parameters.
en.explanation: The caller's positional parameters are saved for the function call and restored when it finishes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions

en.statement: During a function call, Bash changes $0 to the name of the function being executed.
en.explanation: A function call leaves $0 holding the shell or script identity.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions

en.statement: Inside a function, Bash handles exit 7 by ending the call and resuming its caller.
en.explanation: exit terminates the shell executing the function.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions and exit

en.statement: For f(){ true; false; }, Bash reports a failure status when f reaches the end of its body.
en.explanation: A function reaching its closing brace returns its last executed command's status, here the failure from false.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions

en.statement: With global x=old, f(){ declare x=new; }; f changes the global x to new.
en.explanation: Inside a function, plain declare creates a variable local to that call; declare -g selects global scope.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: declare

en.statement: For g(){ printf %s "$x"; } and f(){ local x=inner; g; }, Bash prints inner when f runs.
en.explanation: Bash's dynamic scope makes a caller's local x visible to the helper it invokes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions

en.statement: With global x=outer, f(){ local x=inner; x=changed; }; f leaves the global x equal to outer.
en.explanation: Assignments target f's local x. After f returns, the earlier global binding is visible again.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions

en.statement: Bash applies a positive FUNCNEST limit separately to the recursion depth of individual functions.
en.explanation: FUNCNEST limits the total depth of active function calls, including chains through different functions.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions and FUNCNEST

en.statement: With indexed a=([2]=old) and $1=a inside f, Bash's scalar local -n ref=$1 makes ref[2]=x change a[2].
en.explanation: The local scalar nameref points to the array named by the argument, so assignment through ref[2] reaches a[2].

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameters and Namerefs

en.statement: For f(){ local -; shopt -s nullglob; }, Bash returns nullglob to its earlier off state when f ends.
en.explanation: local - restores options changed through set. This shopt change persists, so nullglob remains enabled after f returns.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: local builtin

en.statement: With value writable, Bash reports failure for value=$(false).
en.explanation: An assignment-only command uses the last command substitution's status. The failing false therefore makes this assignment report failure.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Simple Command Expansion

en.statement: For false | true; :, Bash leaves PIPESTATUS holding the earlier pipeline's results.
en.explanation: The simple command : replaces PIPESTATUS with its own successful status. Read or save pipeline results before executing another command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: PIPESTATUS

en.statement: In false && true, Bash takes the list's status from the final written command true.
en.explanation: The failed false causes && to skip true. The list reports its last executed command's status, which is false's failure.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Lists

en.statement: Bash reaches printf x when it executes the command list true || false && printf x.
en.explanation: The && and || list operators share precedence and associate leftward. Bash evaluates true || false before applying && printf x.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Lists

en.statement: Bash reports success for ! true | true because the last true succeeds.
en.explanation: The leading ! negates the status of the entire pipeline. Both true commands succeed, so ! true | true yields a failure status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

en.statement: With pipefail disabled, Bash selects false's failure as the result of false | true.
en.explanation: A pipeline uses its final command's status when pipefail is disabled. The final true makes false | true succeed.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

en.statement: With pipefail enabled, Bash selects the middle command's status in (exit 7) | (exit 9) | true.
en.explanation: pipefail selects the rightmost nonzero command status. The middle command supplies 9, the selected failure in this pipeline.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

en.statement: Immediately after (exit 7) | (exit 9), Bash exposes PIPESTATUS values 7 and 9 in command order.
en.explanation: PIPESTATUS holds a status for each command in the foreground pipeline. These two commands supply 7 and 9, in pipeline order.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: PIPESTATUS

en.statement: For (exit 7) & p=$!; wait "$p", Bash makes wait return the successful launch status.
en.explanation: wait "$p" returns the child's termination status, 7. Launching the asynchronous command reports a separate successful status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: wait builtin and Lists

en.statement: With set -u and zero positional parameters, Bash treats "$@" as an unset-parameter error.
en.explanation: nounset exempts the special parameter @. Bash accepts this expansion even when its positional-parameter list is empty.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: nounset

en.statement: With set -e and an ERR trap, Bash runs the trap for false in if false; then :; fi.
en.explanation: A failure used as an if condition is exempt from ERR and errexit. Bash completes this if statement with the trap unexecuted.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin and trap builtin

en.statement: With set -e, Bash reaches printf x when it executes false || printf x.
en.explanation: The nonfinal command in this || list is exempt from errexit. Its failure selects printf x as the recovery command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

en.statement: With set -e, Bash exits before printf x in ! true; printf x.
en.explanation: Bash ignores errexit for a pipeline whose status is inverted with !. This script therefore continues to printf x.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

en.statement: With set -e, Bash exits before printf x in f(){ false; printf x; }; if f; then :; fi.
en.explanation: Calling f as an if condition makes Bash ignore errexit throughout that function body. The false is followed by printf x.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit

en.statement: With set -e -o pipefail, Bash exits before printf x in false | true; printf x.
en.explanation: pipefail makes this untested pipeline fail. errexit acts on that pipeline status and exits before the following printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errexit and pipefail

en.statement: With set -e and inherit_errexit enabled, Bash stops before the inner printf in value=$(false; printf x).
en.explanation: inherit_errexit carries -e into this substitution's subshell. The untested false stops that subshell before its printf command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: shopt builtin: inherit_errexit

en.statement: With set -e and n=0, Bash exits before printf x in ((n++)); printf x.
en.explanation: The arithmetic command evaluates n's old value, zero, and returns status 1. errexit stops this untested sequence before printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arithmetic Commands and set builtin

en.statement: With set -e, Bash uses false's failure as local's status in f(){ local value=$(false); }; f.
en.explanation: A valid local declaration returns its own successful status, masking the substitution's failure. errexit therefore continues past local in this call.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: local builtin and set builtin

en.statement: With set -u and x unset, Bash passes an empty argument to printf '%s' "$x".
en.explanation: Expanding an unset scalar as "$x" under nounset causes an error. Bash exits before invoking printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: nounset

en.statement: With set -u and x unset, Bash runs printf '%s' "${x-}" successfully.
en.explanation: The guarded ${x-} form handles unset x explicitly. Bash accepts that expansion under nounset and executes printf.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameter Expansion and set builtin

en.statement: After replacing TERM handler 'cleanup' with ':', Bash uses trap - TERM to restore 'cleanup'.
en.explanation: trap - TERM restores the TERM disposition from when Bash started. It does not undo installed handlers one at a time.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

en.statement: After trap '' TERM, Bash passes the ignored TERM disposition to external commands it executes.
en.explanation: An empty trap action makes TERM ignored. External commands launched by Bash start with that ignored disposition.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Signals and trap builtin

en.statement: When Bash catches TERM while awaiting a foreground external command, it runs its TERM trap before that command ends.
en.explanation: Bash defers a trap for a signal it catches during foreground waiting until the external command finishes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Signals

en.statement: When Bash catches trapped TERM during wait for an asynchronous child, wait returns a status greater than 128.
en.explanation: A caught signal interrupts wait with a status greater than 128, after which Bash runs its handler.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Signals

en.statement: Bash runs an installed EXIT trap when the script finishes with status zero.
en.explanation: Finishing with status zero still terminates the shell, so Bash runs the installed EXIT handler.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

en.statement: Bash runs an installed DEBUG trap after a top-level simple command executes.
en.explanation: Bash executes an installed DEBUG action before a top-level simple command runs.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

en.statement: Bash runs an installed RETURN trap after a sourced file finishes executing.
en.explanation: The RETURN event covers completion of a script run by . or source. Bash executes the installed handler as sourcing finishes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: trap builtin

en.statement: With ERR trapped and errtrace off, Bash fires that trap inside f(){ false; :; } when f runs.
en.explanation: With errtrace disabled, an ordinary function does not inherit the caller's ERR trap. Enabling errtrace supplies that inheritance.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: set builtin: errtrace

en.statement: Bash runs its EXIT cleanup trap when SIGKILL terminates the shell.
en.explanation: SIGKILL terminates the process through an uncatchable signal. Bash gets no opportunity to execute an EXIT cleanup handler.

source.title: signal(7): Signal dispositions

en.statement: For exec {fd}>log, Bash assigns fd a descriptor number of 10 or higher.
en.explanation: A {varname} word in place of a descriptor number makes Bash allocate a descriptor of at least 10 and store its number in the variable, so scripts avoid hard-coded numbers.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: REDIRECTION

en.statement: Given descriptor 3 open, Bash closes it for cmd in cmd 3>&-.
en.explanation: A redirection word of - closes the specified descriptor. Thus 3>&- closes descriptor 3 for that command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Duplicating File Descriptors

en.statement: After successful exec 3>log, Bash restores descriptor 3's previous destination for the next command.
en.explanation: With no command argument, exec applies its redirections to the current shell. Descriptor 3 stays connected to log for subsequent commands.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: exec builtin

en.statement: Bash applies the >out redirection in { printf a; printf b; } >out to both printf commands.
en.explanation: A redirection attached to a compound command such as a brace group applies to every command inside it unless one overrides it, so both printf outputs go to out.

source.title: Bash Reference Manual: Compound Commands

en.statement: With targets='one two', Bash opens two output files for : >$targets.
en.explanation: An ordinary redirection target must expand to one word. $targets produces two words, so Bash reports a redirection error instead of opening files.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Redirection

en.statement: With marker=END, Bash uses END as the closing delimiter for <<$marker.
en.explanation: Bash applies quote removal to the delimiter word, rather than parameter expansion. The closing line for <<$marker contains literal $marker.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

en.statement: With name=dev and <<END, Bash removes double quotes from the body line "$name".
en.explanation: Double quotes within an unquoted here-document body remain input characters. Bash expands $name but keeps the quotes, yielding "dev".

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

en.statement: For <<-END, Bash strips leading tab characters from body lines and the delimiter line.
en.explanation: The <<- form removes leading tabs as Bash reads the body and recognizes its ending delimiter. Leading spaces stay in the input.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Documents

en.statement: With value='a b', Bash rejects : <<< $value as an ambiguous redirection.
en.explanation: Bash expands the here-string word without word splitting. The unquoted $value contributes one string containing a b, so this redirection succeeds.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Here Strings

en.statement: After x=old; (x=new), Bash leaves x equal to new in the enclosing shell.
en.explanation: A parenthesized group runs in a subshell, leaving the enclosing x equal to old. A brace group executes in the current shell environment.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands and Command Execution Environment

en.statement: With noclobber enabled, Bash keeps that option enabled when it starts a parenthesized subshell.
en.explanation: A parenthesized subshell starts with a copy of the enclosing shell's options, including the enabled noclobber setting.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Execution Environment

en.statement: Bash treats an opening { attached to the following command name as a brace group delimiter.
en.explanation: Bash recognizes { as a reserved word when a word boundary separates it from the command list, as in { printf x; }.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands

en.statement: With an earlier synchronous pipeline stage still running, Bash resumes its script when the final stage ends.
en.explanation: Bash waits for the participating pipeline commands to terminate before continuing, even when the final command has already finished.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

en.statement: With lastpipe on and job control off, Bash retains value=x from printf 'x\n' | while read -r x; do value=$x; done.
en.explanation: With job control disabled, lastpipe runs this final while loop in the enclosing shell. Its assignment to value persists after the pipeline.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: shopt builtin: lastpipe and Pipelines

en.statement: Inside a parenthesized group, BASHPID identifies a different process from the one identified by $$.
en.explanation: $$ keeps the enclosing shell's process ID inside a parenthesized subshell; BASHPID identifies the current Bash process.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: BASHPID and Special Parameters

en.statement: With job control off and input available on stdin, Bash makes read x & inherit that input stream.
en.explanation: Bash gives an unredirected asynchronous command /dev/null as stdin when job control is disabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Execution Environment

en.statement: Bash expands <(printf x) to a filename argument in printf '%s' <(printf x).
en.explanation: The process substitution inserts a pathname into the command's argument list. The outer printf receives and prints that pathname as text.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution

en.statement: Bash uses the filename from >(cmd) to supply cmd's standard output to the calling command.
en.explanation: Writes to the filename produced by >(cmd) feed cmd's standard input.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution

en.statement: Bash executes the list in <(producer) asynchronously with the command using the resulting filename.
en.explanation: Bash launches the process-substitution list as asynchronous work; completing that list is separate from executing its enclosing command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution

en.statement: With pipefail enabled, Bash reports a failed command for true < <(exit 7).
en.explanation: The outer true returns status zero. The process-substitution child exits separately with status 7, so pipefail leaves the outer command successful.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution and Exit Status

en.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts 'f:' opt -f config stores f in OPTARG.
en.explanation: getopts stores the consumed option argument in OPTARG. For -f config, OPTARG contains config.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin: OPTARG

en.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts 'f:' opt -f value tail leaves OPTIND pointing to value.
en.explanation: After consuming -f and its argument value, getopts sets OPTIND to 3, the position of the next argument tail.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin: OPTIND

en.statement: With OPTIND=1 and set -- -a, getopts 'ab' opt -b assigns b to opt.
en.explanation: Supplying arguments after the result variable makes getopts parse that explicit list. Here it parses -b while the shell's positional parameters hold -a.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin

en.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts ':f:' opt -f assigns : to opt when the argument is missing.
en.explanation: A leading colon selects silent error reporting. For a missing option argument, getopts sets the result variable to : and OPTARG to the option letter.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin: Silent error reporting

en.statement: With OPTIND=3, Bash moves OPTIND to the start when set -- supplies a fresh argument list.
en.explanation: OPTIND retains parser state within the shell. A script resets OPTIND to 1 before parsing a fresh argument list.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts and set builtins

en.statement: For input line a\b, read -r value assigns the literal text a\b to value.
en.explanation: The -r option makes read retain a backslash as input data. The backslash in a\b remains in value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -r

en.statement: For line 'one:two::three', IFS=: read first rest assigns 'two::three' to rest.
en.explanation: When read receives more fields than variable names, it assigns the remaining fields and their intervening delimiters to the last name.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: Field assignment

en.statement: With indexed a=(old), read -a a appends fields from line 'new value' after old.
en.explanation: read -a removes the array's existing elements before assigning the input fields. Here a contains new and value after read.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -a

en.statement: Bash treats '|!' as a complete input delimiter string in read -d '|!' value.
en.explanation: read -d uses the first character of its delimiter argument. Here a | character ends the read.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -d

en.statement: With descriptor 3 supplying ' a b ' plus a newline, read -u 3 stores ' a b ' in REPLY.
en.explanation: read -u 3 reads from descriptor 3. Supplying no variable names selects REPLY, which retains the line's surrounding spaces after the ending delimiter is removed.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -u and REPLY

en.statement: With value writable, Bash makes read -r value succeed for unterminated input 'last' followed by EOF.
en.explanation: read assigns last to value, but encountering EOF before the newline gives read a nonzero status. Data assignment and successful completion are separate outcomes.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: End of file
